beats.caption: At 32-64 GT/s, a signal only survives a few inches of board copper
beats.text: Copper traces lose more signal the longer they are and the higher the frequency. A PCIe Gen5 lane loses about 36 dB end to end before the receiver gives up, and Gen6 has even less margin. In a big AI server the GPU, CPU, NIC and SSD sit too far apart, so the bits reach the end as mush.

beats.caption: A retimer sits halfway and sends a fresh copy
beats.text: A retimer is a small chip placed in the middle of the link. It fully receives the weak signal, decides each bit, and retransmits it at full strength with a clean clock. Each side now only has to cover half the distance, so the loss budget resets.

beats.caption: Inside: equalize, recover the clock, decide, retransmit
beats.text: Every lane has its own receiver with an equalizer that undoes the channel's blur, a clock-data recovery (CDR) loop that locks onto the incoming bits, and a transmitter. Because it takes part in link training like a real endpoint, it also resets jitter. A simple redriver only amplifies, noise and all.

beats.caption: A nearly closed eye in, a wide-open eye out
beats.text: Engineers judge a link by its eye diagram: many bits overlaid. A tall, wide opening means the receiver can tell ones from zeros easily. At the far end of a long trace the eye has almost collapsed; after the retimer it is wide open again.

beats.caption: More lanes and faster speeds mean more retimers per server
beats.text: AI servers use retimers between CPUs, GPUs, NICs and SSDs and on riser cards, often several per accelerator, and each speed step shortens reach further. That makes it a fast-growing attach product. Related: Astera Labs (ALAB), Broadcom (AVGO), Marvell (MRVL), Credo (CRDO).
